title: Time-Based Key-Value Store: map of key to sorted(timestamp, value), binary search.
shortTitle: Time-Based Key-Value Store: map of key to sorted (timestamp, value) with binary search
keyPoints: HashMap from key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs kept in increasing timestamp order
set() appends a new entry in O(1) amortized since timestamps arrive in increasing order
get() binary-searches the list for the largest timestamp not exceeding the query time (floor search)
Floor boundary logic: when mid timestamp <= query, record it as candidate and move right; when > query, move left
O(log n) per get for a key with n entries; O(1) amortized per set
Off-by-one in the floor search returns the wrong historical value, which is unacceptable in audits

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep each key's history sorted by time and binary-search for the latest entry at or before the query timestamp to answer point-in-time lookups fast.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Time-Based Key-Value Store** – set a value for a key at a given timestamp; get the value that was current at or before a query timestamp.
- **Internal structure** – a HashMap from each key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs in increasing timestamp order.
- **Set operation** – appends a new entry in O(1) amortized because timestamps arrive in increasing order.
- **Get operation** – binary-searches the list for the largest timestamp not exceeding the query (a floor search).
- **Complexity** – O(1) amortized set, O(log n) get for a key with n entries.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India records the published interest rate for each product every time it changes, stamped with the date and time. Later, an auditor asks what the rate was as of last Tuesday noon. The clerk flips to the product's history, which is sorted by time, and quickly jumps to the latest entry on or before Tuesday noon rather than reading the whole history.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A time-based key-value store lets you set a value for a key at a specific timestamp and later query the value that was in effect at or before any given time. Internally it is a HashMap from each key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs kept in increasing timestamp order. Set appends in O(1), and get binary-searches the list for the largest timestamp not exceeding the query.

The floor binary search is the core of the get operation. When the midpoint timestamp is at most the query, you record it as a candidate and move right to look for a later valid entry. When it exceeds the query, you move left. Getting this boundary logic wrong by even one comparison returns the wrong historical value, which in an audit context is unacceptable.

The assumption that timestamps arrive in increasing order is what makes appending keep the list sorted for free. If timestamps can arrive out of order, use a TreeMap per key instead, which keeps entries sorted automatically with O(log n) set and floorEntry for the get.

At the National Bank of India, interest rates for products change over time, and the full history is retained for dispute resolution. Modeling each product's rate history as a time-sorted list and binary-searching it turns what would be a long scan into a fast logarithmic jump. This keeps auditor tooling responsive even when thousands of point-in-time checks run against long histories.

Remember one sentence: store each key's history sorted by time and binary-search for the floor entry to answer point-in-time lookups in O(log n).
